**ABSTRACT**

Selective colleges are sites of social closure. Scholarship examines how selective colleges evaluate applicants, but colleges do not passively accept applications. They recruit. If college recruiting territories are structured by shared infrastructures, then mechanisms of social closure operate upstream of admissions. This article examines how College Board Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model structure high school recruiting visits by selective colleges. Geomarkets carve metropolitan areas into smaller geographic units meant to define local recruiting territories. The Market Segment Model predicts how student demand varies by Geomarket as a function of social class. These market devices become embedded in organizational structures and in third-party products that produce college recruiting behavior. We analyze high school recruiting visits made in 2017 by 42 selective colleges to address three research questions. We find that visit patterns are consistent with the Market Segment Model, with visits concentrated in affluent Geomarkets (RQ1); Geomarkets explain substantial variation in which high schools receive visits (RQ2); and the benefits of being located in a popular Geomarket accrue disproportionately to affluent schools and to schools with moderate shares of Black, Hispanic, and Native students (RQ3). The market devices that college admissions offices incorporate constitute a shared infrastructure that performs social closure by matching a socioeconomic hierarchy of communities to a socioeconomic hierarchy of colleges prior to the evaluation of applications. More broadly, our findings suggest that market devices can facilitate infrastructural collusion, whereby shared reliance on third-party classificatory infrastructures produces coordinated behavior without explicit coordination.

> The hierarchical structure of collegiate competition largely reflects the stratified social and economic dimensions of the communities from which colleges draw their students. Competition among colleges, as admissions officers have told us for so long, is in fact, a matter of keeping company with one’s peers [@RN4982]

Selective colleges are sites of social closure. They confer access to scarce credentials and networks that facilitate entry into privileged occupations [@RN4935], while enrolling student bodies that remain sharply stratified by class and race [@RN4722; @abramitzky2024gi]. @RN4982 observes that competition between colleges occurs within "collective markets," defined by socioeconomic homophily, whereby like-colleges compete for like students on the basis of class. The Consortium on Financing Higher Education (COFHE) -- a group of selective, private colleges -- is one such collective market. "What every envious admissions officer outside the Consortium understands," @RN4982 [p. 45] write, "is that these thirty institutions are strengthened by their very collectivity, though they are in fact one another's principal competitors." With support from College Board, Zemsky developed these observations into market devices for colleges that intervene on the college choice process of students. 
<!--[COMMENT: FOR "INTRODUCE A PUZZLE" FRAMING TO WORK, NEED TO SORTA NAME/CONVEY A DIFFERENT GROUP/MOTIVATION FOR SOCIAL CLOSURE. IT'S SORTA LIKE PATRONAGE SOCIAL CLOSURE OR PEER-PATRONAGE SOCIAL CLOSURE]. -->


Existing explanations of social closure emphasize exclusionary strategies of status groups that redefine admissions criteria in ways that benefit the privileged group [@RN3544; @RN3547] and then diffuse to other colleges \[CITE BROADER LITERATURE\]. Another literature traces legal and policy debates over race-conscious admissions [@warikoo_2025]. These explanations center the admissions process. But colleges do not passively accept applications. They recruit [@RN3519]. The markets they recruit from are not given, they are constructed. If college recruiting territories are structured by shared recruiting infrastructures, then the mechanisms of social closure operate upstream of admissions, raising questions about how recruiting territories are defined and made actionable for colleges.

College recruiting efforts depend on third-party "market devices" that classify high schools and communities on behalf of colleges looking for students. Market devices are tools that calculate and classify. They become incorporated into organizational goals and routines in ways that produce a menu of possible and likely actions. Market devices engender classification situations @RN4810\], whereby a vertical hierarchy of products is matched to a vertical hierarchy of consumers. We argue that Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model -- developed by Zemsky with support from College Board -- are market devices that match "collective markets" of selective colleges to affluent communities, performing social closure upstream of admissions.

Geomarkes carve metropolitan areas into smaller geographic units meant to define local recruiting territories. The Market Segment Model categorized students into four market segments that are a function of class. @RN4982 argue that selective colleges primarily enroll students from high-income, college-educated households, but the relative abundance of these students differs across Geomarkets. Over time, Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model became embedded in college organizational structures and in shared infrastructure colleges draw from. Because affluent Geomarkets concentrate the students selective colleges are looking for, this infrastructure systematically directs recruiting attention toward wealthy communities.

This study examines how Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model structure high school recruiting visits by a sample of 42 colleges -- 14 selective private research universities, 12 selective private liberal arts colleges, and 16 public research universities. While selective private colleges are understood as instruments of intergenerational class transmission, public research universities have been engines of social mobility. However, state disenvestment encourages public research universities to search for nonresident tuition revenue in the same set of affluent Geomarkets as their private peers.

Analyses are guided by three research questions. First, to what extent are visit patterns consistent with recommendations from the Market Segment Model? To what extent do Geomarkets explain which high schools receive recruiting visits? How does Geomarket popularity -- measured as number of visits per high school -- mediate the relationship between school socioeconomic and racial/ethnic composition and the probability of a school receiving a visit?

For the selective private -- and most public -- colleges in our sample, the Market Segment Model recommends focusing on affluent Geomarkets located in regions where students are likely to consider a college like yours [@RN4982]. Although a small number of (mostly public) colleges follow an in-state recruiting strategy, most colleges in our sample follow a national recruiting strategy, in which the majority of visits are to schools outside their home region (e.g., New England). Visits by private colleges -- and out-of-state visits by public universities -- are highly concentrated in affluent Geomarkets. With respect to RQ2, fixed effects regression models find that Geomarkets explain substantial variation in recruiting visits even after controlling for a strong set of school- and neighbohood-level controls. With respect to RQ3, regression models find that schools with a low share of free/reduced lunch students benefit more from being located in a popular geomarket than schools with a high share of free/reduced lunch and schools with a modest share of Black/Hispanic students benefit more from being located in a popular Geomarket than schools with a high share of Black/Hispanic enrollment. Drawing from @RN4808, a wealthy, preominantly white school in a wealthy, predominantly white Geomarket is a "good match" with what selective colleges expect.<!--, whereas poor, predominantly Black/Hispanic school in a wealthy Geomarket is not a good match -->

We make targeted contributions to the sociology of education and a broader contribution to the mechanisms of social closure. Scholarship on selective college access focuses on conflict over admissions criteria and who benefits \[CITE\], while scholarship on enrollment management shows that colleges devote substantial resources identifying and recruiting applicants \[CITE\]. Both literatures center colleges as protagonists, ignoring business-facing intermediaries that classify students on behalf of colleges. Our research points to an upstream ecosystem of third-party vendors, products, and professional associations that that collectively construct the infrastructure that colleges utilize to plan and implement recruiting strategy. Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model were grafted atop the history of racial and class segregation and became embedded within third-party products and college organizational structures. These market devices contribute to social closure by facilitating a tiered matching of colleges to places, encouraging selective private colleges to target high-income localities nationwide, while working class communities are left to less selective institutions. Although public research universities were engines of social mobility in the era of strong state funding, the desire to increase nonresident enrollment encourages to encourages public research universities to target the same set of affluent Geomarkets coveted by selective private institutions. <!-- delete cuz redundancy. Therefore, Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model contribute to social closure by engendering an infrastructure that matches schools and communities to colleges based on socioeconomic privilege. -->

The manuscript is organized as follows. First, we review scholarship on college access and enrollment management. Second, we describe the case of Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model. Third, we develop a theoretical framework based on market devices and classification situations. Fourth, we describe data and methods. Fifth, we present results. Finally, we discuss implications for scholarship. Scholarship at the intersection of quantification and education has considered consumer-facing intermediaries (e.g., college rankings) that discipline consumers and, in turn, businesses \[CITE\]. However, intermediaries that classify consumers on behalf of businesses are more pervasive and more sophisticated [@RN5015]. In the education industry, these intemediaries match ordinally arranged consumers to ordinally arranged products. We argue that sociology of education can develop novel insights by shifting the object of inquiry from students and direct providers education (schools, and colleges) to the market devices that classify students for direct providers.

# Literature Review: College Access in the Enrollment Economy

We situate this manuscript within the broader organizational sociology of higher education, which draws from core paradigms in the sociology of organizations [@RN4738] to ask how the internal, local, and maxro external environment shapes the organizational priorities and behaviors of colleges [@RN2377; @RN4517; @RN2356; @RN1776; @RN4004;@RN2101; @RN515]. Scholarship finds that colleges are highly responsive to changing macro-institutions in the organizational field (e.g., neo-liberalism, market-logics, rankings, affirmative action bans). Scholarship on academic capitalism [@RN2101] in institutional logics [@thornton1999] find that colleges respond to neoliberal legislation and private sector encroachment prioritizing revenue generation and adopting practices associated with for-profit firms [@RN2406] [CITE MORE]. Colleges respond to the growing salience of rankings by elevating rankings relative to other organizational priorities (e.g., social mobility) and adopting practices designed to move up in the rankings [@RN1149; @RN539; @RN2376]. 

Within this organizational tradition, we contribute to scholarship on the supply side of college access. In his study of California adult education, @RN2401[p. 332] defined the "enrollment economy" as reliance on student enrollment for organizational stability: "The most important pressures on these schools in their day-to-day administration arise from the *enrollment economy* \ldots Financial support from the state is figured by the hours of attendance logged the previous year \ldots and a major slump in attendance constitutes a serious threat to organizational welfare." (p. 332). @RN1549 [p. 17] describes the enrollment economy of selective private colleges: "the technology of producing much of what is sold in higher education is unusual in that colleges can buy important inputs to their production only from the customers who buy their products; that is, higher education uses a customer-input technology." Colleges depend on enrolled students for tuition revenue and on alumni for donation revenue. They depend on enrolled students for peer learning effects. Furthermore, the characteristics of enrolled students -- for example, average SAT scores -- substantially determine their national ranking, which then determines student demand for the subsequent cohort of prospects \[CITE\] and also affects research funding and donation revenue \[CITE\].

In the enrollment economy, organizational stability is the responsibility of enrollment management (EM). The EM profession integrates techniques from marketing and economics in order to "influence the characteristics and the size of enrolled student bodies" [@RN2771, p. xiv]. Like product managers, enrollment managers care about customer acquisition and retention, with particular customer segments in mind. As an administrative structure, the "office of enrollment management" typically controls and coordinate the functional activities of admissions, financial aid, and recruiting [@RN2406; @RN3625]. The administrative structure of EM offers one means of categorizing scholarship about the supply-side of college access. A robust literature in the sociology of education examines how colleges, especially selective colleges, adapt their admissions processes in response to external pressures and which applicants benefit [@RN3544; @RN3547; @RN4874; @RN2294; @warikoo_2025; @RN3541; @grodsky_warren_felts_2008; @RN1749; @RN5003; @RN5103; @RN4993; @RN4131]. By contrast, the economics of education emphasizes financial aid policy and how students respond to financial aid [@RN2241; @RN3133; @RN1948]. A growing literature on recruiting examines how colleges identify and cultivate prospective applicants before admissions evaluation occurs.  Several monographs analyze recruiting as part of broader studies [@RN3519; @RN4324; @RN4407; @cottom2017lower]. From the student perspective, @RN4324 finds that underrepresented students were drawn to colleges that made them feel wanted, often attending institutions with lower graduation rates and requiring larger loans than other college options. @cottom2017lower shows that for-profit colleges found a niche in Black and Latinx communities because traditional colleges ignored these communities.

Scholarship on recruiting emphasizes relationships between colleges and high schools. @RN3519 highlights the relational function of recruiting visits to high schools. During the autumn "travel season," admissions officers visit selected high schools across the country "to spread word of the institution and maintain relationships with guidance counselors" because "the College's reputation and the quality of its applicant pool are dependent upon its connections with high schools nationwide" (pp. 53-54). A causal analysis by @haygood_cooper_2026 estimated that when University of Alabama recruiters visited a town, about 8\% more students from that town graduated from the university five years later. @RN4758 argue that off-campus recruiting visits are an indicator of college enrollment priorities. Analyzing recruiting visits by 15 public research universities, @RN4758 found that 12 universities made more visits to out-of-state schools than in-state schools. These out-of-state visits focused on affluent, predominantly white public high schools. Analyzing out-of-state recruiting visits to Los Angeles and Dallas by four public research universities, @RN4759 found that universities engage in "recruitment redlining -- the circuitous avoidance of predominantly Black and Latinx communities along recruiting visit paths" (p. 585). A recruiting visit indicates a social relationship between a college and a high school, suggesting that the college wants to enroll some students from the high school and the high school wants to send some students to the college. @RN5023 conduct a social network analysis of recruiting visits to private high schools by a sample of public research universities and selective private research universities. Analyses revealed extensive overlap in the recruiting networks of public and private universities.

Scholarship on the supply side of college access builds from theoretical perspectives -- institutional theory, resource dependence theory -- that emphasize populations of colleges as decision-making entities that adopt behaviors in response to common external pressures in the organizational field (e.g., rankings, market-encroachment, accountability) [CITE]. These paradigms from the sociology of organizations do not direct the gaze upstream to products and vendors that structure the behavior of colleges. In the economic sociology subfield, the market devices literature focuses on tools incorporated in organizational practices that structure which students receive attention from which colleges. Whereas the growing salience of rankings and market-like behavior is associated with external pressures in the 1990s, we examine market devices creates from a collaboration by a UPenn professor, a member association of selective private colleges, and the College Board. @RN4982 developed two market devices -- Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model -- that commensurated communities as sources of demand for different kinds of colleges. Over time, Geomarkets became incorporated in EM professional practices and software, to the point that they became infrastructure [@RN5082]. We move supply-side scholarship on college access upstream to ask how this shared geography, built around class differences in college choice, shapes which high schools receive recruiting visits.

<!-- CUT TEXT

Scholarship on the supply side of college access shows how individual colleges respond to common pressures for revenue and prestige in deciding whom to recruit and admit. Even when studies examine many colleges, they generally explain recruiting behavior in terms of how each college pursues its enrollment goals. This focus gives less attention to the vendors and products that classify students and communities on behalf of colleges. The market devices literature in economic sociology offers a way to examine how such classifications enter into organizational decisions [@RN5064; @RN4810]. By the time scholars were documenting academic capitalism in the 1990s [@RN2101], colleges had already helped build a shared geography for recruiting. In a collaboration that began in 1978, researchers worked with a consortium of selective private colleges and College Board to develop two market devices, Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model, that made communities comparable as sources of student demand [@RN4982]. Geomarkets became part of the infrastructure of recruiting as admissions offices used the same boundaries to assign staff territories and plan travel through recruiting software [@RN5082]. We move supply-side scholarship on college access upstream to ask how this shared geography, built around class differences in college choice, shapes which high schools receive recruiting visits.

HESE ARE MY HOOK PARAGRAPHS:
dUpon review, scholarship locates inequality in college access in the behavior of households, schools, and colleges \[CITE\]. Scholarship on the supply-side of college access -- selective admissions, EM, recruiting -- argues that students are sorted by the actions of colleges, which are conditioned by macro-institutions in the organizational field \[CITE\]. This focus on college behavior understates the role of third-parties that mediate between consumers and sellers. Sociology of education has investigated intermediaries that "occupy the interface between consumers and producers" [@RN5065, p. 1], including scholarship on college rankings [@RN5003] and school rankings [@RN5005; @RN5075; @hasankumar2019Digitization]. To our knowledge, intermediaries that classify consumers on behalf of sellers have rarely been the object of empirical research [but see @RN5039]. Although consumer-facing intermediaries are salient to media outlets and researchers, intermediaries that classify consumers for businesses are more sophisticated, pervasive [@RN4957; @RN5064; @RN5073; @RN4808], and may be highly salient to professionals responsible for recruiting customers. Scholarship on college access has ignored the infrastructural mechanism of third-party enrollment management tools that classify students and localities on behalf of colleges. These tools -- which are built atop the foundation of segregation in American communities -- facilitate a tiered matching of colleges to places by encouraging selective private colleges and public research universities target high-income localities nationwide, while encouraging less selective institutions to target nearby working- and middle-class communities.

Geomarkets were conceived in service of a class-based model of college choice [@RN4982]. Subsequently, Geomarkets became the basis of College Board Enrollment Planning Service (EPS) software that helped colleges plan recruiting efforts and an organizing principle allocating admissions personnel to recruiting territories. We conceptualize these tools as "market devices" [@callon1998embeddedness] that create "classification situations" [@RN4810], whereby an ordinal hierarchy of students is matched to an ordinal hierarchy of postsecondary institutions. Performativity is the idea that market devices are used in ways that create the behaviors they predict [@RN5067]. Empirically, we show that Geomarkets explain substantial variation of high school visits by a sample of selective private colleges and public research universities, even after controlling for a strong set of school- and neighborhood-level covariates. Finally, we contribute to a critical sociology of the College Board. Existing scholarship focuses on College Board's consumer-facing testing products \[CITE\], mirroring the blind-spot observed in scholarship on intermediaries. This manuscript shows that College Board testing products are the basis for business-facing products that classify prospective students on behalf of colleges.


# Literature Review: College Access in the Enrollment Economy [OLD]

Social closure, associated with Max Weber \[CITE\], is the process by which advantaged groups maintain their privilege by restricting access to resources and opportunities that confer economic and social privilege. Weber conceived of social closure as competition between status groups, defined of "associational communities comprised of all who share a sense of status equality" [@RN3547, p. 3] based on membership of a characteristic (e.g., racial, ethnic, religious, social) that may be the basis of exclusion. Following the transition to rational-legal authority defined by universalistic bureacracies, organizations that confer economic and social privileges become the site of contestation between dominant groups seeking exclusionary closure and marginalized groups seeking usurptionary closure. Colleges are the exemplar site of contestation [@RN865]. Weber states,

> The development of the diploma from universities \ldots make for the formation of a privileged stratum in bureaus and in offices. Such certificates support their holders’\ldots claims to monopolize socially and economically advantageous positions. When we hear from all sides the demand for an introduction of regular curricula and special examinations, the reason behind it is, of course, not a suddenly awakened ‘thirst for education’ but the desire for restricting the supply for these positions and their monopolization by the owners of educational certificates\ldots As the acquisition of the educational certificate requires considerable expense and a period of waiting for full remuneration, this striving means a setback for talent (charisma) in favor of property.

In the U.S., selective colleges confer access to privileged social and economic positions. As college access expands to previously excluded populations, scholarship in sociology and economics document growth in the benefits of graduating from a selective institution [@RN4935; @RN2190], and growth in competition for access to selective institutions \[CITE\]. Based on data from the IRS, the "Mobility Report Cards" [@chetty2020mobility] measures both parental household income and student earnings post-graduation at the college level for students who were born in 1991 and were freshman around 2009. Although low-income students students who graduate from selective colleges have strong labor market outcomes [@RN4722], access to selective institutions is dominated by weealthy households. For example, at Colorado College, one of the colleges in our analysis sample, median family income was about \$379,000 (2026 CPI), with just 2% of freshman coming from the bottom income quintile, 78% of freshman coming from the top quintile, 54% of freshman from the top 5%, and 24% of freshman from the top 1% [@chetty2020mobility].

Several literatures in the sociology of education have analyzed the admissions criteria utilized by selective colleges and which applicants these criteria benefit. The Weberian status group social closure tradition is articulated by the historical sociology of [@RN3544; @RN3547]. Leaders of Ivy League institutions were themselves members of the elite Protestant status group and had an interest in blocking Jewish enrollment growth by developing "character" admissions criteria associated with distinctly upper-class Protestant activities and traits. \[TRANSITION?\] A robust literature analyzes the rise and fall of affirmative action [@RN4874; @RN2294; @warikoo_2025; @RN3541]. Another literature ties the growing importance of SAT/ACT scores in selective college admissions to the rise of college rankings systems that reward colleges for enrolling high-scoring students [@grodsky_warren_felts_2008; @RN1749; @RN5003]. Recent scholarship examines the implementation of "test optional" policies [@RN5103] and holistic admissions processes that evaluate applicants with respect to the opportunities available in their local context \[CITE BASTEDO\]. Although these studies offer rich accounts of how colleges evaluate applicants, the scholarly preoccupation with selective admissions obscures the basic fact that overwhelming majority of colleges -- including most selective colleges -- cannot thrive by passively receiving applications.

The "enrollment economy" refers to reliance on student enrollment for organizational stability. The concept was introduced by @RN2401 \[p. 332\], in his analysis of California adult education institutions: "The most important pressures on these schools in their day-to-day administration arise from the *enrollment economy* \ldots Financial support from the state is figured by the hours of attendance logged the previous year \ldots and a major slump in attendance constitutes a serious threat to organizational welfare." (p. 332). At the opposite end of the prestige spectrum, @RN1549 [p. 17] describes dependence on students by selective private colleges: "the technology of producing much of what is sold in higher education is unusual in that colleges can buy important inputs to their production only from the customers who buy their products; that is, higher education uses a customer-input technology. Colleges depend on enrolled students for tuition revenue and on alumni for donation revenue. They depend on enrolled students for peer learning effects. Furthermore, the characteristics of enrolled students -- for example, average SAT scores -- substantially determine their national ranking, which then determines student demand for the subsequent cohort of prospects \[CITE\] and also affects research funding and donation revenue \[CITE\].

Organizational stability in the enrollment economy is the responsibility of enrollment management (EM). As a profession, EM integrates techniques from marketing and economics in order to "influence the characteristics and the size of enrolled student bodies" [@RN2771, p. xiv]. As an administrative structure, the "office of enrollment management" typically controls and coordinate the functional activities of admissions, financial aid, and recruiting [@RN2406; @RN3625].[^1] The administrative structure of EM offers one means of categorizing scholarship about the supply-side of college access. Accross disciplines, the majority of scholarship focuses on admissions [e.g., @RN4874; @RN4993; @RN4131; @RN3522] or on financial aid [e.g., @RN3133; @RN3762]. These literatures offers less insight into how colleges identify and cultivate prospective applicants before admissions evaluation occurs. Therefore, a growing literature in sociology analyzes the earlier "recruiting" stages of acquiring "leads," and soliciting "inquiries" and applications \[CITE\]. Several monographs analyze recruiting as part of broader studies on enrollment management [@RN3519], high school to college transitions [@RN4324], elite reproduction [@RN4407], or political economy [@cottom2017lower]. From the student perspective, @RN4324 finds that underrepresented students were drawn to colleges that made them feel wanted, often attending institutions with lower graduation rates and requiring larger loans than other college options. @cottom2017lower shows that for-profit colleges found a niche in Black and Latinx communities because traditional colleges ignored these communities.

[^1]: @RN2406 exemplifies a literature at the intersection of EM and organizational behavior that shows how concerns about the enrollment economy motivate changes in organizational behavior, such as diversifying degree programs or changing the name of the organization [@RN869; @RN515; @RN2518]

@RN3519 provides an ethnography of enrollment management at a selective private liberal arts college. Being tuition-dependent and sensitive about its position in the rankings, The College focuses on enrollment goals related to academic profile and revenue generation. @RN3519 highlights the relational function of off-campus recruiting visits: "the College's reputation and the quality of its applicant pool are dependent upon its connections with high schools nationwide" (p. 54). During the autumn "travel season," admissions officers visit selected high schools across the country "to spread word of the institution and maintain relationships with guidance counselors" (p. 53-54). @RN4741 reported that "calling high school counselors after visits" was an effective and widely-used outreach strategy for both private universities and public universities. Thus, relationship maintenance remains a high-touch process even in the digital age. The College tended to visit the same "feeder" schools year after year because recruiting depends on long-term relationships. Visited schools tend to be affluent schools -- in particular, private schools -- that possess the resources to host a visit and enroll high-achieving students who can afford tuition.

Whereas scholars in the sociology of education have investigated recruiting as part of a broader analysis, AUTHORS [-@RN4758; -@RN4759; -@RN5023] have attempted to develop a literature that makes college recruiting behavior the object of empirical analysis. @RN4758 argue that off-campus recruiting visits are a credible indicator of college enrollment priorities.[^2] [INSERT SENTENCES SAYING HOW MUCH IS SPENT ON OFF-CAMPUS RECRUITING AND SCHOLARSHIP ON THE EFFECTS OF OFF-CAMPUS RECRUITING]. @RN4758 analyzed recruiting visits made by public research universities. The authors found that 12 of the 15 universities made more visits to out-of-state schools than in-state schools. These out-of-state visits focused on affluent, predominantly white public high schools. Set against scholarship about nonresident enrollment growth as a response to declining state support [@RN3753; @RN3685], these results suggest that many public research universities prioritize enrollment from wealthy out-of-state students.

[^2]: Sociological theories of organizational behavior argue that organizations expend substantial resources on goals they care about while symbolically adopting -- highly visible, ceremonial behavior with few resources expending -- goals demanded by stakeholders in the broader institutional environment \[CITE\].

@RN5023 conduct a social network analysis of recruiting visits to private high schools by a sample of public research universities and selective private research universities. A visit indicates a social relationship between a college and a high school, suggesting that the college wants to enroll some students from the high school and the high school wants to send some students to the college. Both public and private universities made a disproportionately large number of visits to private schools relative to public schools. She found that universities engage in "recruitment redlining -- the circuitous avoidance of predominantly Black and Latinx communities along recruiting visit paths" (p. 585).

Upon review, scholarship locates inequality in college access in the behavior of households, schools, and colleges \[CITE\]. Scholarship on the supply-side of college access -- selective admissions, EM, recruiting -- argues that students are sorted by the actions of colleges, which are conditioned by macro-institutions in the organizational field \[CITE\]. This focus on college behavior understates the role of third-parties that mediate between consumers and sellers. Sociology of education has investigated intermediaries that "occupy the interface between consumers and producers" [@RN5065, p. 1], including scholarship on college rankings [@RN5003] and school rankings [@RN5005; @RN5075; @hasankumar2019Digitization]. To our knowledge, intermediaries that classify consumers on behalf of sellers have rarely been the object of empirical research [but see @RN5039]. Although consumer-facing intermediaries are salient to media outlets and researchers, intermediaries that classify consumers for businesses are more sophisticated, pervasive [@RN4957; @RN5064; @RN5073; @RN4808], and may be highly salient to professionals responsible for recruiting customers. Scholarship on college access has ignored the infrastructural mechanism of third-party enrollment management tools that classify students and localities on behalf of colleges. These tools -- which are built atop the foundation of segregation in American communities -- facilitate a tiered matching of colleges to places by encouraging selective private colleges and public research universities target high-income localities nationwide, while encouraging less selective institutions to target nearby working- and middle-class communities.

Geomarkets were conceived in service of a class-based model of college choice [@RN4982]. Subsequently, Geomarkets became the basis of College Board Enrollment Planning Service (EPS) software that helped colleges plan recruiting efforts and an organizing principle allocating admissions personnel to recruiting territories. We conceptualize these tools as "market devices" [@callon1998embeddedness] that create "classification situations" [@RN4810], whereby an ordinal hierarchy of students is matched to an ordinal hierarchy of postsecondary institutions. Performativity is the idea that market devices are used in ways that create the behaviors they predict [@RN5067]. Empirically, we show that Geomarkets explain substantial variation of high school visits by a sample of selective private colleges and public research universities, even after controlling for a strong set of school- and neighborhood-level covariates. Finally, we contribute to a critical sociology of the College Board. Existing scholarship focuses on College Board's consumer-facing testing products \[CITE\], mirroring the blind-spot observed in scholarship on intermediaries. This manuscript shows that College Board testing products are the basis for business-facing products that classify prospective students on behalf of colleges.

# Theory and Case

## Theory

**Market devices**. The market devices literature examines how the components of markets are assembled and enacted, and how these processes shape behavior [@callon1998embeddedness; @RN5064; @RN5067]. Market devices are tools for calculating, comparing, and classifying (e.g., algorithms, metrics, rankings) that become incorporated into products and transactions "that make economic action possible" [@RN4777, p. 1176]. @RN5064 [p. 2] define market devices as a "way of referring to the material and discursive assemblages that intervene in the construction of markets." Here, material refers to tools and technologies, like spreadsheets or software, while discursive refers to representational elements, such as categorical, quantitative, and ordinal variables. An assemblage refers to a bundle of heterogeneous components that work together, suggesting that market devices consist of and build upon other market devices. 

Commensuration is "the expression or measurement -- of characteristics normally represented by different units -- according to a common metric" [@RN5063, p. 315]. The process of commensuration defines which objects can be compared on the basis of which metrics. Objects previously compared on the basis of many characteristics may be compared using a single metric. The creation of metrics facilitates the comparison of objects previously deemed incomparable. Market devices incorporate commensuration to facilitate decision-making based on simple metrics. For example, college rankings enable prospective students to compare colleges based on a single metric. @RN5005 analyze UK school "league tables," a commensurating market device that facilitated comparisons among schools on the basis of standardized test scores. Similarly, the SAT is a commensurating market device that enabled colleges to compare students from different schools, overcoming the problem that information on a high school transcript "is relative to a standard that a college will not understand unless it draws very often from the high school" [@RN2247, p. 103]. In turn, College Board Geomarkets are a commensurating market device built atop the SAT that enabled colleges to compare the attractiveness of different recruiting markets.

In the market devices framework, neither market devices nor actors have agency in isolation. Whereas market devices are tools, "agencement" refers to an arrangement of market devices, actors, practices, and organizational goals and pressures that creates the capacity for action in a particular context [@RN5102]. Agencement is akin to potential energy that tends toward particular directions due to the design of the tools and the orientations of actors wielding them. This arrangement makes some courses of action available, recognizable as choices, and more likely than others. In the contemporary "market configuration" [@RN4517] of U.S. higher education, defined by state disinvestment, college rankings, and competition for paying customers, college enrollment goals may prioritize "full-pay" and/or high-achieving students. In turn, third-party recruiting products (e.g., Student Search Service by College Board, Enroll360 by EAB, Intersect by PowerSchool, Slate by Technolutions) incorporate classifications and metrics that help colleges identify, compare, and target prospective students, schools, and territories in pursuit of enrollment goals. Together, these tools, the actors using them, and organizational practices such as territory assignment and planning high school visits form an agencement.

Theories (e.g., pricing theory, status attainment theory), by themselves, are not market devices. They are abstract ideas that can be applied to specific contexts. For example, homophily is the idea that people who share similar characteristics are more likely to connect [@mcpherson2001birds]. Theories become part of market devices when components of the theory are embedded within the device. Performativity is the idea that theories of market behavior do not merely describe behavior; rather, market devices are constructed and acted upon in ways that bring about behavior consistent with the theory [@RN5064; @RN5067]. Whereas homophily is often described as a natural behavior, @RN4975 argues that commercial social networks engineer homophily by developing friend-and-follow recommendation algorithms based on similarity metrics (e.g., shared attributes, behaviors, and network positions). Performativity may also be tied to the origins of a market device. Market devices are often created by people within specific social structures, who are oriented towards a common culture, world view, or status group [@RN5067; @mullerseitz2012maneuvering]. These actors may design market devices based on specific theories and understandings of market behavior. Once incorporated into commercial products and practices, these arrangements become available to users beyond the groups that created them, carrying their categories and operating assumptions into new settings.

**Classification situations**. @RN4810 that processes of ordinalization "endogenous to the market" (p. 560) define class based on the consumption side of the economy. "Classification situations" are processes in business-to-consumer markets whereby businesses "sort and slot people [consumers] into new types of categories \ldots with different economic rewards or punishments attached to them" [@RN4810, p. 561]. The canonical example is credit scores [@RN4877], which enable third-party intermediaries on supply side to "slice consumers into behaviorally-defined risk groups, and price offerings to them accordingly" [@RN4810, p. 560]. Ordinalization refers to ranked tiers. Organizations seek "good matches" between ordinally classified products and consumers, aiming to link "a wealthy customer with a quality credit card, or a heavy drinker with a bad insurance plan" [@RN4808, p. 17]. In consumer markets defined by status, products acquire status by identifying with a high-status customer base while consumers signal status by identifying with particular products [@RN1228; @RN1045; @RN1549]. Therefore, classification situations reinforce cultural homophily by linking tiers of consumers to corresponding tiers of sellers.
<!-- 
Whereas Marxist acounts define social class from the production side of the economy (e.g., owner, laborer), @RN4810 draw from Weber to argue that processes of ordinalization "endogenous to the market" (p. 560) define class based on the consumption side of the economy. 

On the demand side, consumers find themselves \ldots fitting into these categories -- which, by design, are not constructed from standard demographic classifications such as race" [@RN4810, p. 560] but are highly correlated with social categories. -->

Because classification situations create expectations about the characteristics of actors assigned to assigned to particular categories, actors may receive different treatment depending on how closely they match the ideal-type of the category. An anecdote by @RN5072 [pp. 20-21] highlights the the role of "good matches" between ordinally classified products and ordinally classified customers

> One of the authors had a credit card transaction denied while trying to refill her car’s gas tank in a high-poverty Oakland neighborhood. The clerk indicated with resigned anger that the location of his gas station was the likely cause of the problem. Back in Berkeley a few minutes later, the card worked without a hitch.

The episode illustrates how a person's apparent fit with a classified context can become consequential for treatment. An affluent school with predominantly White or Asian enrollment in an affluent Geomarket may be perceived as a good match because it exemplifies the schools recruiters expect to find. By contrast, schools whose socioeconomic or racial composition departs from those expectations may not share equally in the recruiting attention directed toward the Geomarket.

## The Case: Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model

In 1978, amid concerns about the declining college-age population, University of Pennsylvania president Martin Meyerson asked professor Robert Zemsky, “Who thinks about Penn?” and “What other institutions do they think about when they think about us?” [@RN4982, p. x]. To answer these questions, Zemsky began working with the Market Research Committee of the Consortium on Financing Higher Education (COFHE), a group of 30 selective private institutions with a tradition of sharing data on their applicant pools [@RN4982, p. x]. The project sought to “capture and quantify” the practical knowledge of admissions officers [@RN4982, p. 11]. As the authors recall, “Much of this project’s framework -- the Market Segment Model and its derivation from admissions officers’ folklore -- was shaped and then reshaped in our discussions with members of the committee” [@RN4982, p. x]. The project grew into an effort to predict student demand for any college from any locality. College Board underwrote the project and provided score-sending data for all 1980 SAT test-takers [@RN4982]. The collaboration between this network of selective colleges and College Board produced two, linked market devices. Geomarkets classified places into community-based enrollment markets intended to define recruiting territories. The Market Segment Model classified prospective students into groups based on where they sent their SAT scores [@RN4982, pp. 4, 11–12].

The initial task was to define geographic boundaries “in a manner consistent with admissions officers’ intuitive understanding of student pools” [@RN4982, p. 4]. As one admissions officer put it, "'There are only three kinds of college-bound students: those who want to live at home, those who want to live on campus but bring their laundry home, and those who want to go far enough from home that Mom and Dad can’t visit without calling first'" [@RN4982, p. 11]. The researchers drew boundaries at three geographic levels, which they called “region, state, and community” [@RN4982, p. 11]. The project initially covered New England, Middle States, and the South. Within those regions, the researchers “divided each state into as few as two and as many as thirty community-based enrollment markets or pools, for a total of 143 separate markets” [@RN4982, p. 11]. These community-level markets became known as Geomarkets. The authors briefly described how they drew the boundaries.

> In many cases, the market boundaries match formal political and educational divisions, reflecting natural channels of communication. Each major metropolitan area is composed of several markets, usually corresponding to the inner city, a first ring of suburbs, and an outer ring of suburbs. [@RN4982, pp. 11–12]

The Market Segment Model classified students by where they sent their SAT scores relative to their home Geomarket. Students send SAT scores to colleges they are considering. For a given student, each college receiving a score was classified as local (in the student’s Geomarket), in-state (elsewhere in the same state), regional (in another state in the same region), or national (outside the student’s region). The model then assigned the student to one of four market segments based on which category received the largest number of their score sends. For example, a student was classified as local if they sent more scores to colleges in their own Geomarket than to colleges in any one of the other three categories [@RN4982]. The authors state that the Market Segment Model was "nothing more than a set of simple rules for disaggregating high school seniors into similar groups. The model worked because students, once so disaggregated, appeared to behave in remarkably consistent ways" [@RN4982, p. 4].


@RN4982 found that four variables -- parental education, family income, scholarstic aptitude, and educational aspirations -- predicted student market segment. These four variables "reflect the basic social patterns of the nation; it would have been surprising if these were not the four social variables that best explained the patterns of college choice" [@RN4982, p. 33]. Next, the authors conduct a social network analysis that defines colleges as competitors if many students send scores to both colleges. The analysis reveals that "collegiate competition occurs principally between like institutions" [@RN4982, p. 46] as defined by the social class of their customers. @RN4982[p. 72] conclude that "the layering of collegiate competition is primarily a socioeconomic layering. The hierarchical structure of collegiate competition largely reflects the stratified social and economic dimensions of the communities from which colleges draw their students." In turn, these findings yielded practical implications for college recruiting. Selective colleges mostly enroll students from the national and regional market segments, who tended to come from more affluent, college-educated households. However, Geomarkets differ in the relative abundance of students with particular socioeconomic characteristics. @RN4982 [p. 42] recommend that colleges seeking students in the regional and national segments target Geomarkets with many students already “predisposed toward institutions such as your own".

> On occasion, senior spokespersons for the profession worry that students outside the main \[Geo\]market areas remain forgotten and hence, unchallenged. Inevitably, the increasing competition for students, the expense of travel and mailings, and internal political constraints compel institutions to concentrate their efforts where they will do the most good. The result is a natural reinforcing of the basic socioeconomic patterns that gave shape in the first place to the structure of college choice.

In 1984, College Board created the Enrollment Planning Service (EPS), a recruiting product sold to colleges that was based on Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model [@RN4987; @RN4980]. EPS expanded the original 143 Geomarkets to 304 nationwide [@RN5016]. In 1995, 37 percent of four-year public institutions and 49 percent of four-year private institutions used EPS [@RN5021]. Building on @RN4982, EPS initially offered two reports for each Geomarket.  The Market Segment Profile showed the number of students in each market segment, their socioeconomic characteristics, and their average test scores. The Institutional Profile showed how many students in each segment sent scores to a particular college. Recruiters could obtain this report for their own institution or for a competitor [@RN4982; @RN4980]. Typical @RN5019 marketing material describes EPS as, "the marketing software that pinpoints the schools and Geomarkets where your best prospects are most likely to be found. With the click of a mouse, EPS provides you with comprehensive reports on your markets, your position in those markets, and your competition." Following @RN4982, the EPS platform encouraged users to, first, identify promising Geomarkets and, second, to identify desirable high schools for recruiting visits. To find new recruiting territories, EPS encouraged colleges to select peer institutions and identify Geomarkets where many students had sent scores to those institutions. Recruiters could then examine the score-sending behavior of students at individual high schools within promising Geomarkets to decide which schools to visit [@RN5019; @eps_whitepaper_2019]. 

Although Geomarkets were initially designed to approximate the territories of admissions officers [@RN4982], Geomarkets have become an organizing principle which admissions offices define recruiting territories and assign them to officers. On background, admissions officers and EM consultants told us that Geomarkets became part of the shorthand lexicon of the National Association of College Admissions Officers (NACAC). Admissions officers might introduce themselves by saying, "I recruit 'PA 2'," referring to the "Chester County, PA" Geomarket. We find evidence for this claim in the LinkedIn profiles of admissions officers. Examples include: "Personally managed schools in Indiana geomarkets 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, & 9" [@warren_linkedin_geomarkets_2026]; "Led recruitment efforts in geomarket MA06, the greater metro Boston area" [@porter_linkedin_geomarket_ma06_2026]; and "increased applications from the Long Island geomarket NY 16 - NY 21 for the 2021 admission cycle by 18.3%" [@montecalvo_linkedin_geomarkets_2026]. Institutional materials also incorporate Geomarkets. A report from the Dartmouth College Admissions Ambassador Program lists the number of interviewers and applicants by Geomarket [@dartmouth_aap_geomarkets]. The University of Chicago, for example, lists separate recruiting assignments for the “IL 9 -- North Shore” and “IL 12 -- South and Southwest Suburbs” Geomarkets [@Chicago-Office-of-College-Admissions:aa].
<!-- These assignments bring Geomarkets into the recruiting agencement by linking a set of schools to the officer responsible for recruiting there [don't like this sentence]. -->

Colleges also use Geomarkets to organize recruiting territories in their customer relationship management (CRM) systems. CRMs help sellers manage interactions with current and prospective customers. Commercial CRMs such as Salesforce and Oracle incorporate geographic territories that are meaningful to the product being sold so that sales staff and customer records can be assigned to those territories. @RN4982 created Geomarkets because knowledge about recruiting territories was known only by veteran admissions officers (pp. 9-11). Today, Slate is the leading higher education CRM, used by more than 2,000 colleges [@technolutions_enterprise_crm_2026]. Slate incorporates Geomarket codes into high school and prospect records [@slate_geomarket_screenshots_2026]. Admissions offices can assign recruiters to Geomarkets [@technolutions_staff_assignments_2026] and recruiters can plan visits to high schools and college fairs within their assigned territories [@technolutions_college_fairs_2026]. The LinkedIn profile of an admissions officer states, "Utilized Slate to create territory management tools for the recruitment team. Generated reports broken down by state and geomarket and sorted by high school to reflect applicant/admit/deposit data for past 3 cycles" [@james_linkedin_slate_geomarkets_2026]. Similarly, Oracle’s PeopleSoft Campus Solutions CRM also incorporates Geomarkets [@RN5017]. Therefore, a geographic classification meant to approximate the tacit knowledge of admissions officers became embedded in the systems colleges use to organize recruiting work.
<!-- "In college recruitment," @RN4982[p. 10] write, "knowing the territory means understanding which students within which communities are most likely to be attracted to your college."  -->


## Research Questions and Expected Results

Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model are two linked market devices developed within an elite network of selective colleges in collaboration with College Board [@RN4982, p. x]. Both built on the SAT, which gave colleges a common measure for comparing students from different high school systems [@RN2247, p. 103]. Geomarkets defined recruiting territories, and the model used SAT score sends to make those territories comparable as sources of demand for different kinds of colleges. In contrast to scholarship that views race- and class-based inequality in educational attainment as a function of historically-based structural inequality [CITE], the Market Segment Model is based on the idea that class-based differences in student college choice are natural. The model advises colleges to target Geomarkets and schools that already showed interest in institutions like theirs, resulting in a "natural reinforcing of the basic socioeconomic patterns that gave shape in the first place to the structure of college choice" [@RN4982, p. 44]. EPS wrapped Geomarkets and the Market Segment Model into a tool for recruitment planning. By incorporating Geomarkets into admissions CRMs (e.g., Slate) and the territories assigned to admissions officers, Geomarkets became part of the agencement through which colleges pursue enrollment goals. Performativity is the idea that market devices are constructed and utilized in ways that bring about behavior consistent with theories of market behavior. In @RN5067, predictions from the Black-Scholes model became more accurate over time because traders began embedding components of the model into spreadsheets and software [finish sentence]. In the context of college recruiting, colleges may utilize Geomarkets, EPS, and related infrastructure to decide which schools to visit.

Our first research question asks, to what extent high school recruiting visits are consistent with recommendations from the Market Segment Model? The model advises colleges to recruit in Geomarkets where many students already consider institutions like theirs [@RN4982]. Selective private colleges primarily draw from the regional and national market segments, whose students tend to come from affluent, college-educated households concentrated in particular Geomarkets [@RN4982, pp. 33, 42]. Directing visits toward places with strong prior demand can reinforce disparities in who has direct contact with selective colleges. If those visits also sustain student interest, the resulting demand can feed back into subsequent recruiting decisions [@RN4794, p. 224]. We expect selective private colleges and public research universities seeking nonresident students to concentrate their visits in regional or national markets, depending on how far afield they draw students. We also expect them to visit high schools disproportionately in affluent Geomarkets.

Our first research question asks, to what extent high school recruiting visits are consistent with recommendations from the Market Segment Model? According to @RN4982, selective private colleges primarily depend on students from the regional and national market segments. Further, regional and national students tend to come from affluent, college-educated households. Affluent households are not scattered randomly across the country, but rather clump together in particular geographic communities. Like UK "league tables" [@RN5005], Geomarkets are a means of commensurating geographically disparate localities in terms of the number of students from each market segment. For selective private colleges and public universities pursuing nonresident students, the Market Segment Model recommends focusing on affluent Geomarkets located in regions where many students are likely to consider a college like yours [@RN4982]. We predict most colleges in our sample will adhere to a regional or national (but not an in-state) recruiting strategy, depending on whether they have regional or national enrollment demand. We also predict that colleges will disproportionately visit high schools located in affluent Geomarkets. We answer RQ1 using simple descriptive statistics. 

Because the patterns examined in RQ1 could reflect a general tendency to visit affluent places, our second research question asks whether Geomarkets help explain which high schools receive recruiting visits after accounting for finer-grained measures of school and neighborhood socioeconomic composition. Geomarkets are part of the recruiting agencement through which colleges assign staff and plan travel. When an admissions officer is assigned a Geomarket, its boundaries help define which schools the officer considers when planning visits. Colleges may also assign more recruiters per resident to affluent Geomarkets. The University of Chicago, for example, lists one recruiter each for “IL 9 -- North Shore” and “IL 12 -- South and Southwest Suburbs” [@Chicago-Office-of-College-Admissions:aa]. Relative to their 2020 populations of about 161,000 and 1.2 million, respectively, the North Shore assignment represents roughly 7.5 times as many recruiters per resident. We therefore expect the probability that a given college visits a high school to vary across Geomarkets, even among schools with similar characteristics in the same state.

Our third research question asks whether the relationship between Geomarket popularity and a school’s probability of receiving a recruiting visit depends on the school’s socioeconomic and racial composition. @RN4808 argue that the goal of classification situations is to make "good matches" between ordinally classified products and ordinally classified consumers. @RN4808 [p. 17] write that "‘good matches’ are perceived as natural because they fit well with how things already are." In college recruiting, the priorities that draw recruiters to a Geomarket may also guide which schools they visit within it.  An affluent school in an affluent Geomarket is a good match because it exemplifies the kind of schools that draw recruiters to the Geomarket. By contrast, a poor or predominantly Black/Hispanic school in an affluent Geomarket does not match expectations and may not reap the same locational benefits. We measure Geomarket popularity as the number of recruiting visits per high school in the Geomarket. We expect schools serving more affluent students and schools with smaller shares of Black and Hispanic students to benefit more from being located in a popular Geomarket.

## Data and Sample

**Sample of colleges**. This manuscript draws from a data collection that tracked off-campus recruiting visits made during the 2017 calendar year by a convenience sample of colleges. The data collection sample consisted of: all public research-extensive universities as defined by the 2000 Carnegie Classification (N=102), all private universities in the top 100 of the 20XX U.S. News and World Report National Universities rankings (N=57), and all private colleges in the top 50 of the 20XX U.S. News and World Report Liberal Arts Colleges rankings (N=47). The rationale for different criteria for inclusion across different university types is because these criteria reflected the interest of a foundation that funded the data collection.

For universities in our data collection sample, we investigated their admissions website for pages that posted their upcoming off-campus recruiting visits. For institutions that posted such pages, we scraped the pages once per week throughout 2017.[^5] Many universities in our data collection sample only posted certain kinds of events (e.g., hotel receptions and national college fairs) but not others (e.g., day-time visits to high schools). These institutions were excluded from the analysis sample. The final analysis sample for this article consists of 16 public research universities, 14 private selective research universities, and 12 private seletive liberal arts colleges that we believed posted all varieties of off-campus recruiting events on their admissions website.[^6]
